turns.t: I'm only here because the health visitor insisted. I've been a bit thirsty lately, that's all, it's nothing really.
Right, well I'm glad she did. How long has the thirst been going on?
Two weeks, give or take. I just put it down to being up in the night with the baby.
Could be. Is it worse at any particular time, or all day?
All day, really. I keep a bottle by the sofa. It's honestly fine.
Okay. Any blurred vision, with it? Print going fuzzy, that sort of thing?
No, my eyes are all right.
Good. Let's go through what you're taking. Your notes say metformin, is that still right?
Yes, metformin. 500 mg, twice a day, with food.
Twice a day, every day?
Every day, yes.
Honestly, now. Most new mums miss some, and nobody will tell you off.
Well... the evening one, sometimes. When the baby's fussing at bedtime, it slips my mind. Maybe two or three nights a week.
Thank you, that's useful to know. I'm not worried by it, I just need the real picture.
It's not a big deal, is it?
It matters a little, which is why I'm asking. Your records also show you had gestational diabetes in your pregnancy.
Yes, that's right. They told me it might go away after the birth.
It often does, but it can come back, which is why we recheck. And you've an underactive thyroid too, for about five years?
Five years, yes. That's all quiet, it never bothers me.
Good. Let me take your blood pressure and check your weight on the scales.
Go on then. I've not dared step on them since the birth.
Blood pressure is 124/78. And your weight is 84 kg.
Eighty-four. Well, it could be worse.
That's no bad figure at all. Slip your shoes and socks off, I'll check your feet and ankles.
Do I have to? My feet are a state.
I've seen worse, I promise. Just let me look.
There's no swelling around the ankles, and the skin on your feet looks healthy.
Told you, nothing wrong.
So here are the options. One, we carry on as we are and do nothing more. Two, we check your sugar control with a blood test. Three, we change what you're taking.
Which one would you go for?
The second. I'd like to arrange an HbA1c blood test, which shows your average sugar over the last few months. The nurse can do it before you leave.
Fine, if you think it's needed.
I do. Then we decide about the tablets once we have the number.
And if it's high?
Then we talk about options again: the dose, a different tablet, or more help with food and exercise. No decisions today.
All right. Is it all right to keep taking the metformin meanwhile?
Yes, carry on with it, and try to build in the evening dose. Put it next to the baby's bottles, so you trip over it.
That's actually clever. I'll do that.
I'd like to see you again in three months, once the results are back and we've decided.
Three months. I'll put it in the calendar.
Reception will book it as you leave. Walking with the pram is a good start for exercise, by the way.
I do walk to the shops most days. The baby likes it.
Then you're ahead of most. Keep drinking water for the thirst, rather than juice.
Right. Water only. Boring, but fine.
If the thirst gets much worse, or you start passing a lot more urine, ring us before the three months.
I will, though I'm sure it won't.
Does your partner help at night, so you can get some sleep?
Some nights. He sleeps through the baby, it's almost a talent.
Ha. Then make him do the evening bottle, so you can rest. Any other questions?
No, that's everything. Thank you.
Good. Off you go, and congratulations on the little one.
Thanks very much. Cheerio.

chief_complaint.value: I've been a bit thirsty lately

physical_examination.finding: the skin on your feet looks healthy

clinical_actions.description: Take the evening metformin dose by linking it to a routine; drink water for the thirst

clinical_uncertainties.description: Patient says she takes metformin twice a day but sometimes misses the evening dose.
